extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator / early-18th-century English literate public (gentlemen, clergy, moralists)
extracted.subtask_description: Producing short, periodical moral and satirical essays (Spectator-style) that comment on social manners, religion, and private vices using anecdote and light satire. Emphasizes normative judgments about character and conduct illustrated by examples and types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stages of drowsiness as social portrait
rubrics_metrics.description: A humorous, quasi-clinical sequence of the progressive symptoms of a habitual sleeper (dullness, drowsiness, yawning, nodding, sleeping, snoring, turning, recovering posture, stretching, awaking, calling for small-beer) that is presented as a natural picture of the lives of many honest English gentlemen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a concrete, chronological list of small habits to satirically characterize a social type. The anecdote of 'Nicholas Hart' (periodical fits of sleeping, with the exact day-by-day progression) is given as a model. The passage treats such men as 'Drones without Stings'—innocuous but useless—suggesting the comedic value of cataloguing mundane repetition as characteristic of a class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of earning by flattering great rather than industry
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrasts honest industry with making a livelihood by sleeping or by rendering agreeable companionship to the great (i.e., flattering patrons), implying moral censure of earning through dependence on favour rather than work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Nicholas Hart anecdote is used to show that Rest can procure sustenance, and this is compared to poets 'sleeping on Parnassus'—the essayist suggests suspicion of those who prosper by pleasing the great rather than by industry. Use ironic comparison to classical examples (e.g., Juvenal) and concrete contemporary anecdotes to make the moral point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting false zeal: pride, interest, or ill-nature
rubrics_metrics.description: When one calls his behaviour 'zeal' for religion or opinion, it is often motivated by pride, interest, or ill-nature rather than genuine devotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advise readers to 'examine his Heart thoroughly' — look for signs such as setting oneself above others, seeking proselytes as social proof, or using religion to justify malice. Examples: zealous defenders who maintain friendships with immoral men provided they agree in belief; zeal used as cover for persecution. Treat identification of motives as the primary diagnostic.

rubrics_metrics.name: True zeal must promote morality, not persecution
rubrics_metrics.description: Genuine zeal is laudable only when it advances morality and the happiness of mankind; zeal that results in imprisonment, confiscation, torture, or bloodshed is vain and criminal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast 'zeal for advancing Morality' with instruments like 'Racks and Gibbets, Gallies and Dungeons.' If zeal employs violence or destroys families, the essayist pronounces the religion unprofitable. Use historical examples of massacres born of 'pretended Zeal' to show consequences and to mark the boundary between laudable and pernicious zeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritise moral wrongs over speculative difference
rubrics_metrics.description: A true zeal should be 'much more angry with a Sinner than a Heretick'—i.e., moral failings deserve greater censure than mere differences in speculative opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a criterion to judge religiously motivated anger: distinguish moral infractions (which harm others) from doctrinal disputes. Encourage tempering doctrinal zeal with compassion and a sense of proportion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency and self-reflection for opponents of religion
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism of religion (infidelity/atheism) should not be carried on with the same spirit of rancour and bigotry as religious zeal; atheists who zealously propagate irreligion are guilty of the same follies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out the absurdity of being 'zealous for Irreligion' and 'bigotted' about nonsense; urge critics to be consistent and avoid the same temperamental faults (fierceness, contention, wrath) they ascribe to zealots. Use satire ('Gamesters ... eternally upon the Fret') to expose the vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge religion by its effects on morality and social order
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if hypothetical errors existed in a religion, its value can be assessed by whether it 'so effectually contribute[s] to the heightning of Morality.' The practical moral outcomes (virtue, trust, love of neighbour, self-discipline) are key measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support religious claims not only by doctrinal proof but by appeal to their moral fruits (examples from St. Paul). Invoke historical exemplars (Pythagoras, Socrates, Xenophon's prince) to show that adherence to established worship and religion correlates with 'Wisdom and Virtue.' Use pragmatic, consequentialist argumentation as rhetorical strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of infidelity: ignorance, vanity, and love of pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Contends that many infidels arise from lack of virtuous education or from vanity (desire to appear wiser) or an aversion to restraints that religion imposes on pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When criticizing unbelievers, attribute motives wisely: consider whether skepticism stems from poor instruction, intellectual vanity, or self-interest. Use this diagnosis to rebut infidelity as resulting from character defects rather than superior reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognising the Jilt: characteristic behaviours and types
rubrics_metrics.description: Defines the 'Jilt' as a species of woman who delights in tormenting lovers through alternating coldness and familiarity, artful negligence, artificial intrigues, and a pleasure in making others uneasy; classifies types (e.g., Hyæna — indolent inattention; Biblis — purchases admirers of others; Chloe — inconstant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide vivid, concrete anecdotes (Kitty, Hyæna, Biblis, Chloe) to illustrate patterns: false glances, careless conduct masking calculation, writing perplexing letters, using unknown hands, and manipulating admirers. Use typology and narrative examples as a practical guide for recognizing and satirizing the type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical advice to suitors: prefer decency and honour
rubrics_metrics.description: Men are advised to avoid women who are insincere jilt-types and to 'converse with none but those who lived within the Rules of Decency and Honour'; to adopt regular behaviour (visits, assemblies) as a strategy for finding suitable partners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggest behavioural reforms for men (appearances of steadiness, attending assemblies, making proper visits) and to judge potential partners by consistent decency and honour rather than by romping wit or fashionable irregularity. Use personal narrative (author's own misfortunes) to ground the counsel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of praise: esteem of the worthy over popular applause
rubrics_metrics.description: One should prefer 'the Testimony of a good Conscience' and approbation from deserving, intelligent peers rather than general, promiscuous applause from the multitude; the praise of ignorant men is mere good-will, not a reliable measure of merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating acclaim, consider the character and judgment of the person commending you; avoid pandering to the crowd. Use examples (Lacedaemonians, Phocion) and satire of dedications to ignorant patrons to show the absurdity of seeking fame from the wrong audience. Recommend seeking judgment 'only by his Peers' and treating popular praise as a potential snare.
